scenarios.title: Find the incident window
scenarios.brief: Support says something went wrong for a short time. Check whether the data backs up their report, and find the time window when it happened.

scenarios.title: Server errors after a release
scenarios.brief: HTTP server errors went up after a release. Find the failing endpoint or service, and a typical error.

scenarios.title: An increase in rejected sign-ins
scenarios.brief: More sign-ins are being rejected than usual, but everyday rejections are mixed in. Find the unusual reason and the client it affects.

scenarios.title: Failures after a rolling deployment
scenarios.brief: After a rolling deployment, some of a service's requests fail while others succeed. Find what the failing requests have in common, and when the first failure happened.

scenarios.title: A rare error in a busy service
scenarios.brief: A busy service logs one rare exception that seems linked to failed requests. Find the exception and one request where it happened.

scenarios.title: Fewer requests on a dashboard
scenarios.brief: A dashboard only counts requests that have a value in http.route. That count dropped, but total traffic stayed the same. Find the producer and version that stopped sending http.route.

scenarios.title: Find the log pattern that matters
scenarios.brief: A service logs thousands of repeated warnings. Find the one message pattern that is linked to the failed requests.

scenarios.title: Rank failing routes with ES|QL
scenarios.brief: Rank endpoints by failed request count and failure rate during the incident.

scenarios.title: Compare before and after a release
scenarios.brief: Use numbers to show whether a release really changed latency and errors.

scenarios.title: Compare services in one incident
scenarios.brief: Build one short results table with the volume, failures and p95 latency of each service. p95 is the time that 95% of requests finish within.

scenarios.title: Triage an incident from a dashboard
scenarios.brief: Use the service overview dashboard to quickly find the affected region, service and time period.

scenarios.title: Drill down from a dashboard spike
scenarios.brief: A dashboard chart shows a spike in errors. Drill down to the documents behind it, and keep the chart's filters and time range.

scenarios.title: Inspect two panels that disagree
scenarios.brief: Two dashboard panels seem to disagree. Find out how each one is calculated, and which one answers the incident question.

scenarios.title: Find a slow dependency in a trace
scenarios.brief: Checkout latency is high. Find the downstream dependency and operation that cause it.

scenarios.title: Follow an error through a trace
scenarios.brief: The edge service reports a general failure. Find where the exception started, and how it propagated (spread) to other services.

scenarios.title: Dependency traffic growing faster than users
scenarios.brief: Latency and dependency traffic went up, but user traffic did not. Find out whether retries multiplied the calls.

scenarios.title: Correlate a trace with its logs
scenarios.brief: A failing trace has no error details. Use log correlation to find the exact application log for the request.

scenarios.title: Slowdown during a traffic peak
scenarios.brief: One service slows down during a traffic peak. Find out whether its CPU is saturated (at its limit) at the same time.

scenarios.title: A workload that keeps restarting
scenarios.brief: A workload becomes unstable over several hours. Find the resource trend and the first restart.

scenarios.title: One instance busier than the rest
scenarios.brief: Overall service health hides one outlier instance. Find it, and show that the other instances are still healthy.

scenarios.title: Find the throughput saturation point
scenarios.brief: Latency rises only above a certain throughput (requests per second). Use the evidence to estimate the saturation point, where latency starts to climb.

scenarios.title: Triage an alert you don't know
scenarios.brief: An alert fired for a service you don't know. Decide whether it is an active customer issue, and point to the source events that show it.

scenarios.title: Checkout requests are suddenly slow
scenarios.brief: Users report that checkout became slow in the last few minutes. Find the bottleneck, and back it up with correlated evidence: the same request seen in each service.
